idiom_name: asyncio forwarding task with put_nowait into a bounded tap queue holding a deepcopy
implementation_notes: Python supplies the secondary channel, not the tap. asyncio.Queue is single-consumer - get() removes and returns an item to one waiter - so the tap fans out by interposing a hand-written forwarding coroutine: it reads the channel, puts a snapshot into a bounded tap queue with put_nowait, then awaits the primary put unchanged. put_nowait never suspends; it raises asyncio.QueueFull on a full queue, and that except branch is the only place an explicit, counted drop policy can live (await tap_q.put() would suspend the forwarding task and leak analyzer backpressure into the primary flow). Thread model: everything runs on one event loop - the analyzer is a separate task draining the tap queue, and because the loop executes all tasks in one thread, any CPU-bound analysis done inline delays every task, so heavy inspection belongs in run_in_executor/asyncio.to_thread or another process. Copy semantics: queues pass object references, so deepcopy (or a per-message serializer) before handoff, else analyzer mutations are visible to the receiver. Overflow: tap_q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N); the default maxsize=0 is infinite and hides analyzer lag as memory growth. Choose the asyncio form when producer and consumer are coroutines on one loop; in threaded code keep the same shape with queue.Queue (put_nowait raises queue.Full); choose multiprocessing.Queue when the analyzer must be isolated from loop stalls - its payload is serialized, which is a genuine deep copy, at the cost of the feeder-thread join behaviour. The stdlib analogue is logging: a fixed handler list plus logging.handlers.QueueHandler/QueueListener, but that is LogRecord-specific and its overflow routes through handleError and can drop records silently - for arbitrary messages the tap stays hand-written, and async brokers (e.g. aiokafka) ship no producer interceptor to hook instead.
pitfalls: asyncio.Queue defaults to maxsize=0, which the docs define as infinite: the tap never reports QueueFull, the drop counter stays at zero, and a lagging analyzer surfaces as unbounded memory growth instead of visible loss - set maxsize and count drops in the except branch.

Handing off with await tap_q.put(msg) makes a full tap queue suspend the forwarding coroutine until the analyzer drains it, so the analyzer's latency throttles the primary flow in-band - exactly what a Wire Tap must never do; only put_nowait keeps the handoff non-blocking.

Queues pass references, not copies: without deepcopy or serialization the analyzer and the primary receiver share one object, and copy.deepcopy itself will not copy file, socket or similar types and may copy too much - define an explicit snapshot per message type.

All Tasks run in the event loop's single thread, so a CPU-bound analyzer inspecting inline delays every task and IO operation on that loop no matter what queue fronts it - offload with loop.run_in_executor/asyncio.to_thread or a separate process.

A multiprocessing.Queue tap hands the analyzer a pickled (hence genuinely deep-copied) payload, but a feeder thread transfers buffered items asynchronously: a producer process that is joined before its items are drained hangs (the docs' deadlock example), and qsize() is explicitly unreliable - never treat that queue's counters as proof the tap delivered.
